whatItDoes: Add a 2.579-mill property-tax levy in Boulder County for child care and preschool. It would raise $30 million in tax collection year 2027, with later revenue based on collections. Money would lower families’ costs, raise pay for child-care and preschool teachers and staff, and expand capacity to serve more children. Tax revenue and investment earnings would be exempt from Colorado’s constitutional revenue limits and statutory property-tax limits.
yesMeans: Approve the ongoing property-tax levy for child care and preschool and its revenue-limit exceptions.
noMeans: Do not approve this property-tax increase or its proposed revenue-limit exceptions.

whatItDoes: Allow Eldorado Springs Public Improvement District to borrow up to $1 million, with total repayment capped at $1.44 million and an effective interest rate no higher than 4%, to improve its wastewater-treatment plant and cover related costs and repayment reserves. Borrowing and repayment amounts would be reduced if costs or loan rates are lower than estimated or other funding is secured. Repayment would come from special assessments on benefited properties in Local Improvement District No. 3 and other legally pledged funds. Assessment revenue, investment earnings and earnings on borrowed money would receive a voter-approved revenue-limit exception.
yesMeans: Approve the wastewater-treatment borrowing, repayment from special assessments and other pledged funds, and the revenue-limit exception.
noMeans: Do not authorize this borrowing or the related revenue-limit exception.

whatItDoes: Create Sombrero Ranch Public Improvement District in Boulder County and authorize a property-tax levy of up to 14.47 mills. It would raise $185,000 in tax collection year 2027 and amounts based on the levy afterward. Revenue would resurface county roads and fund other county-road improvements within the district. The district could enter a multiyear financial obligation of up to $3.5 million, paid from the tax and other legally available funds. Tax revenue, other available funding and interest earnings would be exempt from Colorado’s constitutional revenue limits, statutory property-tax limits and other applicable limits.
yesMeans: Approve formation of the district, the property-tax levy, the multiyear obligation and the revenue-limit exceptions.
noMeans: Do not approve forming the district or the proposed taxes, multiyear obligation and revenue-limit exceptions.

whatItDoes: Create Summerlin Public Improvement District in Boulder County and authorize a property-tax levy of up to 17.34 mills. It would raise $60,000 in tax collection year 2027 and amounts based on the levy afterward. Revenue would resurface county roads and fund other county-road improvements within the district. The district could enter a multiyear financial obligation of up to $1.25 million, paid from the tax and other legally available funds. Tax revenue, other available funding and interest earnings would be exempt from Colorado’s constitutional revenue limits, statutory property-tax limits and other applicable limits.
yesMeans: Approve formation of the district, the property-tax levy, the multiyear obligation and the revenue-limit exceptions.
noMeans: Do not approve forming the district or the proposed taxes, multiyear obligation and revenue-limit exceptions.

whatItDoes: Increase the Boulder County Board of Commissioners from three members to five. If approved, five commissioners would take office in January 2029 after the November 2028 election. Question 201 separately asks how the expanded board would be elected.
yesMeans: Expand the board to five commissioners beginning in January 2029.
noMeans: Keep the board at three commissioners.

whatItDoes: Choose how Boulder County’s five-member commission would be elected if voters approve expansion under Question 200. Option 1 elects all five commissioners by district: each must live in the district and only its voters elect that seat. Option 2 elects three commissioners by district and two commissioners countywide, with the two countywide members allowed to live in any district. This is a choice between two methods, rather than a yes-or-no question. The selected method takes effect only if the board expands.

Authorize up to $400 million in Boulder general-obligation debt, with total repayment capped at $650 million, and up to $32.5 million in additional property taxes annually to repay it. Projects include recreation centers, senior-center space, fire stations, police and 911 facilities, the municipal building and the municipal service center. The property-tax rate would have no fixed cap, but annual collections could not exceed the stated limit and could only cover debt payments or repayment reserves. Debt proceeds, reserves, taxes and investment income could be kept and spent outside Colorado’s constitutional revenue limits and other legal limits.
yesMeans: Approve the debt and property taxes for city capital projects and the revenue-limit exception.
noMeans: Do not authorize this borrowing, the additional property taxes or the related revenue-limit exception.

whatItDoes: Change Boulder’s charter to limit city debt to 3% of the actual value of taxable property, instead of calculating the limit using assessed value. The city’s factual explanation says this would allow more borrowing than the current calculation.
yesMeans: Approve calculating the debt limit from actual property value.
noMeans: Keep the existing debt-limit calculation.

whatItDoes: Create an annual $4,000 tax on Boulder homes occupied for 183 days or less per year. The amount would increase with the Denver-Aurora-Lakewood Consumer Price Index, never falling below $4,000 or exceeding $7,000. Estimated revenue is $6 million in 2028, the first full fiscal year of collection, with later revenue based on collections. Money would support city services, including police, fire, parks, recreation, transportation and maintenance. Tax revenue and related earnings could be retained and spent outside Colorado’s constitutional revenue and spending limits.
yesMeans: Approve the vacancy tax and its revenue-limit exception.
noMeans: Do not approve this vacancy tax or its proposed revenue-limit exception.

whatItDoes: Add a charter-guaranteed right for full-time Boulder fire-department employees to bargain collectively over safety, wages, benefits and other employment terms, except matters reserved to management. If negotiations reach an impasse, the process would use nonbinding fact-finding and, if needed, a citywide vote. The city’s explanation says bargaining rights already exist in contract; the measure would put them in the charter.
yesMeans: Put the specified firefighter collective-bargaining rights and impasse process into the charter.
noMeans: Do not add these rights and procedures to the charter.

whatItDoes: Raise $19.5 million in the first full year for Longmont police, fire, 911 dispatch, emergency-support staff, equipment, vehicles and facilities. Add a property-tax levy initially capped at 2.44 mills for collection in 2027, and add 0.33 percentage points to the sales and use tax beginning January 1, 2027. Later revenue could vary with collections. Starting in tax collection year 2028, the property-tax levy could rise to offset specified revenue losses from tax credits, refunds, abatements and changes to property-assessment rates or values. Revenue and investment income could be collected and spent outside Colorado’s constitutional revenue limits and other legal limits.
yesMeans: Approve the public-safety taxes, the specified future levy adjustments and the revenue-limit exception.
noMeans: Do not approve these tax increases, levy adjustments or the related revenue-limit exception.

whatItDoes: Add open-space land to the Longmont charter’s list of land that cannot be sold or transferred without voter approval. Exceptions would cover public roads, utilities, life-essential infrastructure, open-space operations, and sales or transfers of structures on the land.
yesMeans: Require voter approval for open-space land sales or transfers, subject to the listed exceptions.
noMeans: Leave the charter’s existing land-transfer rules unchanged.

whatItDoes: Add a Longmont charter provision to use ranked-choice voting methods where possible to elect future mayors and city council members, starting in November 2029.
yesMeans: Approve using ranked-choice voting where possible beginning in November 2029.
noMeans: Do not add this ranked-choice-voting requirement to the charter.

whatItDoes: If voters also approve ranked-choice voting under Question 3C, realign Longmont council elections so the three at-large seats are elected together in one cycle and the three ward seats together in the next, alternating afterward. During the transition, the at-large seat elected in 2027 and Ward 2 seat elected in 2029 would have two-year terms instead of four-year terms. If Question 3C fails, this realignment would not occur.
yesMeans: Approve the election-cycle change, including the two shortened transition terms, if ranked-choice voting also passes.
noMeans: Do not approve this council-election realignment.

whatItDoes: Extend Louisville’s existing 0.125% historic-preservation sales tax from January 1, 2029 through December 31, 2038. It would raise $1.5 million in 2029 and whatever amounts it produces later. Proceeds, together with the existing 0.125% historic-preservation use tax, would serve historic-preservation purposes previously approved by voters. Starting January 1, 2027, funds could also support city programs and capital projects preserving local history and cultural heritage, and the share for operating and maintaining the museum campus could rise from 20% to 30%. Revenue could be kept and spent outside Colorado’s constitutional revenue limits and other legal limits.
yesMeans: Continue the sales tax through 2038, expand its permitted uses and museum allocation, and approve the revenue-limit exception.
noMeans: Let the historic-preservation sales tax expire at the end of 2028 and do not approve the proposed changes in uses and allocation.

whatItDoes: Expand the Louisville charter’s permitted reasons for closed executive sessions to cover any matter allowed by Colorado’s Open Meetings Law. Allow boards, commissions, task forces and committees to hold such sessions under that law, subject to procedures and limits set by city ordinance. The state law’s restrictions would still apply.
yesMeans: Allow the broader set of legally permitted executive-session topics and procedures.
noMeans: Keep the charter’s existing, narrower executive-session rules.

whatItDoes: Change Louisville’s charter so the mayor and council members take office at the first regular council meeting after election results are certified, instead of the first meeting after the election.
yesMeans: Begin elected officials’ terms after results are certified.
noMeans: Keep the current rule beginning terms at the first meeting after the election.

whatItDoes: Raise the Louisville charter’s signature requirements for citizen petitions. Initiative petitions would need signatures from 7.5% of registered voters instead of 5%; referendum petitions would need 5% instead of 2.5%.
yesMeans: Approve the higher signature thresholds for initiatives and referendums.
noMeans: Keep the existing 5% initiative and 2.5% referendum thresholds.

whatItDoes: Allow Louisville’s public bodies to hold public meetings outside public buildings and facilities, provided every meeting location is accessible to all members of the public.
yesMeans: Allow additional meeting locations that meet the public-access requirement.
noMeans: Keep the current charter limits on meeting locations.

whatItDoes: Require proponents of a citizen-initiated ordinance or charter amendment in Louisville to submit its text to the city manager for review and comment at a public meeting first. City staff could not require changes to the text or impose additional procedural requirements.
yesMeans: Add the public review-and-comment step, with the limits on staff authority.
noMeans: Do not add this review-and-comment requirement.

whatItDoes: Update Louisville’s charter by removing gendered pronouns, replacing references to citizens with members of the public, replacing City offices with the City Clerk’s office and city website, and replacing television with virtually.
yesMeans: Approve these wording changes in the charter.
noMeans: Keep the existing charter wording.

whatItDoes: Continue Lafayette’s existing property tax for Lamont Does Park, which expires in December 2026, through December 31, 2046. It could raise no more than $713,000 annually. Money would fund park and related-facility improvements, operation and maintenance, annually appropriated obligations for those purposes, and related city purposes. Revenue could be collected and spent outside Colorado’s constitutional revenue and spending limits and other legal limits.
yesMeans: Extend the existing park tax through 2046 and approve the revenue-limit exception.
noMeans: Do not extend this tax beyond its existing December 2026 expiration.

whatItDoes: Create a 3.5% lodging tax in Erie starting January 1, 2027. It would apply to hotel and motel rooms, bed-and-breakfasts, short-term rentals and other accommodations for stays of 30 days or less. The tax would raise up to $150,000 initially and whatever it produces annually afterward. Revenue could fund general town purposes, including parks and recreation, infrastructure, and public safety. Tax revenue and investment earnings could be kept and spent outside Colorado’s constitutional revenue limits and other legal limits.
yesMeans: Approve the lodging tax and its revenue-limit exception.
noMeans: Do not approve this lodging tax or its proposed revenue-limit exception.

whatItDoes: Authorize up to $32.5 million in Erie debt, with total repayment capped at $52.6 million, to expand, renovate, equip and maintain the community center. Projects include fitness studios, a gymnasium, racquetball courts, multipurpose space and strength-training areas. Add 0.501 percentage points to the town’s sales and use tax beginning January 1, 2027, raising up to $4,866,857 in the first full fiscal year and amounts based on collections later. Revenue would repay debt and fund community-center construction, operation and maintenance and other town parks and recreation expenses. Bonds could be repaid early with a premium of up to 3%. Revenue, debt proceeds and investment income could be spent outside Colorado’s constitutional revenue limits.
yesMeans: Approve the community-center debt, additional sales and use tax and revenue-limit exception.
noMeans: Do not authorize this debt, additional tax or related revenue-limit exception.

whatItDoes: Add 5.3 mills to Allenspark Fire Protection District’s property-tax rate. It would raise up to $331,000 in fiscal year 2027 and amounts based on collections annually afterward. Money would support fire and emergency response, rebuild reserves, maintain buildings and grounds, replace fire and medical equipment, expand staffing and fire mitigation, provide community outreach and education, and add water storage and dry hydrants. Revenue and earnings would have a permanent exception from Colorado’s constitutional revenue limits and applicable statutory limits.
yesMeans: Approve the additional property taxes for district emergency services and the permanent revenue-limit exceptions.
noMeans: Do not approve this property-tax increase or its proposed permanent revenue-limit exceptions.

whatItDoes: Add a 6-mill property-tax levy in Timberline Fire Protection District, raising $1.2 million in the first full fiscal year and amounts based on the levy annually afterward. Money would support emergency response, including additional firefighters, wildfire mitigation, emergency reserves, general operations and capital needs.
yesMeans: Approve the additional property-tax levy for the district’s response, operations and capital needs.
noMeans: Do not approve this additional property-tax levy.

whatItDoes: Create Niwot as a municipality within the territory described in the incorporation petition. If voters approve, the Boulder County District Court would enter an incorporation order. If voters reject it, no municipality would be created and the incorporation process would end.
yesMeans: Approve incorporation of the proposed municipality.
noMeans: Do not create the proposed municipality.

whatItDoes: Form a nine-member commission to draft a home-rule charter for the proposed municipality of Niwot if incorporation also passes. The draft charter would then need voter approval at a later election.
yesMeans: Approve forming the charter-drafting commission, with its work dependent on incorporation.
noMeans: Do not approve forming this home-rule charter commission.

whatItDoes: If Niwot incorporates, authorize a 2.5% sales and use tax beginning January 1, 2028. It would raise $2.8 million in the first full fiscal year and amounts based on collections later. Revenue could fund capital improvements, operations, debt repayment and any lawful municipal purpose. Groceries for home consumption would be exempt; the municipal government could set other exemptions. Use tax would cover tangible property used, stored or consumed in Niwot, including building materials. The government would have to enact an ordinance before collecting the taxes. Revenue and earnings could be kept and spent outside Colorado’s constitutional revenue limits.
yesMeans: Approve the proposed sales and use tax and its revenue-limit exception if Niwot becomes a municipality.
noMeans: Do not approve this sales and use tax or its proposed revenue-limit exception.

whatItDoes: If Niwot incorporates, authorize a 4-mill property-tax levy for operating and maintenance costs. It would raise $900,000 in the first full fiscal year and amounts based on collections annually afterward. Revenue would be exempt from Colorado’s constitutional revenue limits and the statutory property-tax limit.
yesMeans: Approve the proposed property-tax levy and its revenue-limit exceptions if Niwot becomes a municipality.
noMeans: Do not approve this property-tax levy or its proposed revenue-limit exceptions.

whatItDoes: If Niwot incorporates, authorize a 3% special sales tax on retail marijuana and marijuana products beginning January 1, 2028, in addition to other municipal sales taxes. The measure states $60,000 in the first full fiscal year, with later revenue based on collections. It would apply to sales authorized by state law, and the municipal government would have to enact an ordinance before collecting it. Revenue and earnings could be kept and spent outside Colorado’s constitutional revenue limits.
yesMeans: Approve the additional marijuana sales tax and its revenue-limit exception if Niwot becomes a municipality.
noMeans: Do not approve this special marijuana sales tax or its proposed revenue-limit exception.

whatItDoes: If Niwot incorporates, allow the municipality to keep and spend all revenue counted toward fiscal-year spending, beginning in 2027 and in later years. This includes grants, fees, charges and tax revenue. State revenue and spending limits, including Colorado’s constitutional TABOR limit, would not restrict those collections. The measure itself would not set a new tax rate.
yesMeans: Allow the proposed municipality to retain and spend this revenue outside the specified state limits.
noMeans: Do not approve this exception; the constitutional revenue limit and refund requirement would continue to apply.

whatItDoes: If Niwot incorporates, authorize up to $15 million in debt, with total repayment capped at $28 million, for street, road, bridge, drainage, sidewalk and related transportation repairs, improvements and maintenance. Revenue bonds or other obligations would be paid from sales and use taxes only if voters also approve those taxes under the separate sales-tax measure. Debt proceeds and investment earnings would receive a constitutional revenue-limit exception.
yesMeans: Approve the transportation borrowing and revenue-limit exception, with repayment dependent on separate voter approval of the sales and use tax.
noMeans: Do not authorize this borrowing or the related revenue-limit exception.
